text: Brahehus was built between 1637 and 1660 as a magnificent residence and pleasure house. Strategically located 180 meters above Lake Vättern, it served as a landmark for the County of Visingsborg.

The history of the castle is two-fold: from a glorious period as a representative castle for the nobility, to serving as a place of detention for prisoners of war during the 18th century, before the great fire of 1708 left it as a stone ruin.
Brahehus is built directly on solid bedrock of granite and quartz. According to paranormal theories, these minerals can act as 'batteries' for energy.

The exposed location entails extreme weather conditions. The lashing winds and the cold cliff made the castle difficult to heat, which has shaped the historical accounts of suffering and hardship for both residents and prisoners.

history.heading2: Per Brahe the Younger - Facts & Biography
text: Born: February 18, 1602, at Rydboholm Castle - Died: September 12, 1680, at Bogesund Castle.
Parents: Abraham Brahe and Elsa Gyllenstierna. He belonged to the highest Swedish nobility and was the grandson of Per Brahe the Elder.
Children: Despite two marriages, he had only one child, his daughter Elsa Beata Brahe (1629–1653), born in his first marriage to Kristina Katarina Stenbock. Her early death was a heavy blow to him.

Political career: He served as the Lord High Chancellor of Sweden (the country's highest official after the King) from 1640 to 1680. He was also twice Governor-General of Finland (1637–1640 and 1648–1654), where he implemented extensive reforms. His influence was so great that he was popularly known as 'Count Per'.

Estates: As the Count of Visingsborg, he ruled over a vast area around Lake Vättern. He was one of Sweden's largest landowners and a visionary builder who founded cities, schools, printing houses, and infrastructure.
Born: 1618 - Died: 1650.
Parents: Gustav Eriksson Stenbock and Beata Margareta Brahe. Through her mother, she and Per Brahe were cousins, which was common among the nobility at the time.
Marriage: Married to Per Brahe the Younger in 1628. They had one surviving child together, their daughter Elsa Beata Brahe (1629–1653).

Biography: Kristina Katarina was a central figure in Per Brahe's life. It was for her that he initiated the construction of Brahehus in 1637 as a magnificent bay window and pleasure house. Tragically, she passed away in October 1650, ten years before the castle was fully completed. She is buried in the Brahe Church on Visingsö.
Born: 1612 - Died: 1680.
Parents: Johan Pontusson De la Gardie and Catharina Oxenstierna.
Marriage: First married in 1633 to Field Marshal Lennart Torstenson, with whom she had several children. After his death, she married Per Brahe the Younger in 1653.

Biography: Beata De la Gardie was one of the most influential women of her time. Through her first marriage to one of Sweden's foremost military strategists, Lennart Torstenson, she was deeply involved in the political and military elite of the Great Power Era. When she married Per Brahe in 1653, two of the country's most powerful families were united.

Role at Brahehus: She was the Countess of Visingsborg during the time when Brahehus was most active as a representative castle. Unlike Kristina Katarina's unfinished dream, Beata represents the completed era of the castle's existence. She was an experienced administrator, used to managing large households and navigating the political games at court.
Born: 1633 - Died: 1699.
Parents: Erik Brahe and Elsa Gyllenstierna (the same mother as Per Brahe the Younger, but Erik was Per's brother).

Biography: Nils Brahe the Younger was a Swedish count, privy councillor, and military officer. After his father Erik died in 1638 and his mother in 1643, he was taken under the protection of his uncle, Per Brahe the Younger, and raised by him. He lived in close association with the Lord High Chancellor's influence on Visingsö, which shaped him into the heir who, upon Per Brahe's death in 1680, took over the extensive County of Visingsborg.

Administration and setbacks: Nils inherited an estate in turmoil. He took over responsibility for Brahehus, among other properties, during a transitional period when the Swedish state's 'reduction' under King Charles XI began to dismantle the economic power of the nobility. Nils was forced to witness how the family's immense wealth was gradually confiscated by the Crown, creating an extremely pressured economic situation. His time in power was marked by a constant struggle to try to manage an inheritance that was slipping from the family's grasp.

Although the counts themselves rarely lived at Brahehus, the site was constantly inhabited by guards, stable hands, and servants who maintained the property. Life on the cliff was notoriously harsh, especially during the winter months when icy, lashing winds blew in over Lake Vättern, making the stone building incredibly difficult to keep warm.

history.heading2: Prisoners of War and Dark Fates
text: During Charles XII's wars in the early 18th century, the function of Brahehus changed drastically. What was once a luxurious pleasure house for the nobility was transformed into a place of detention for Russian prisoners of war and wounded soldiers. The luxurious halls were filled with suffering, disease, and desperation.
Conditions for the prisoners on the cold and drafty cliff were extremely harsh, and many did not survive the severe winters. This period of human suffering left deep marks on the site.

The fate of Brahehus was sealed in the autumn of 1708. A violent fire broke out in the adjacent village of Uppgränna, located just below the cliff. Due to strong winds from Lake Vättern, sparks and burning coal fragments were carried up the steep cliffs and landed directly on the shingle roof of Brahehus.

Although the fire was a material catastrophe where the entire interior, the magnificent roof structure, and all inventory were completely destroyed, there is no information that anyone was harmed. The isolated location on the cliff made firefighting efforts impossible, and within a few hours, the building was burnt out.
Since that catastrophic night in 1708, Brahehus has remained a roofless stone ruin, left to the elements as a memory of a bygone golden age.

After the fire, the ruin turned into a resource for the local population in Gränna. Many stonemasons and villagers retrieved material from the razed walls to build their own farms. This has sparked theories that energy from Brahehus might be dispersed in several of the older buildings in Gränna, as the stones that witnessed both the golden age and the catastrophic fire now form the foundations of other people's homes.

To understand the spirits of Brahehus, one must also look across the water to Visingsö and the Brahe Church, where the Brahe family is buried. Per Brahe the Younger and his wife Beata De la Gardie were laid to rest in magnificent copper coffins in the underground burial vault.

In the early 19th century, the burial vault suffered a disrespectful looting. Thieves broke in and forced open Christina's and Per's coffins to steal valuables, jewelry, and precious fabrics. Parts of the deceased's remains were scattered on the floor before the thieves fled. Perhaps the grave desecration and the disturbing of the dead's rest is one of the strongest triggers for spirits becoming restless and returning to the places they loved in life, such as Brahehus.
